title: Here if You Need: Rethinking Education Support Staff Deployment
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This Australian secondary teacher and inclusion coordinator presents their school's evolving approach to deploying Education Support (ES) staff -- moving away from one-to-one tagging models toward a circulating room-support model backed by EEF and SEND research. The article's central evidence base is research showing that constant one-to-one TA presence inadvertently undermines inclusion, independence, and socialization -- what David Didau calls Satnav teaching, where students arrive at the destination without understanding the route. The school's reform has three prongs: removing the one-to-one tag except for students with complex functional needs, improving teacher-to-ES communication before lessons, and providing ES staff with genuine professional learning including a Responsive Teaching PD day. The author extends this with two vivid analogies: the car-speed analogy (both cars make progress but the gap widens) to explain how any-progress-counts misses the point of closing achievement gaps, and the underwear analogy for appropriate fading of scaffolding over time. The piece concludes with advocacy for appreciating ES staff financially and professionally, noting a recent vote against an industrial agreement the author considers undervaluing.
points: * Research shows that untrained and unsupervised TAs providing constant one-to-one support inadvertently undermine inclusion, learning, socialization, and independence -- good intentions create Satnav teaching where students follow procedure without developing understanding. * The appropriate goal of education support is independence, not comfort: support that never fades widens the achievement gap even when both students make progress, because rate of progress is what determines whether gaps close or widen. * The shift from one-to-one tagging to circulation requires teachers to brief ES staff before lessons -- because ES staff, however experienced, have not planned or sequenced the content and cannot substitute for expert teacher guidance. * Professional development for ES staff is often omitted or replaced with admin duties, but including ES staff in high-quality PD (such as a Responsive Teaching day) produces rapid improvement in practice and strong buy-in. * ES staff are emotionally and physically drained by work they are systematically undervalued for -- appreciating them is not just a nicety but a prerequisite for having them function as the instructional spies who see what actually happens in classrooms.
quotes: The ineffective and separate instruction delivered by untrained and unsupervised TAs as well as their constant physical presence inadvertently undermine the inclusion, learning, socialization and independence of students with disabilities, and the pedagogical roles of their teachers. (Sharma and Salend, 2016)

This can lead to what David Didau refers to as Satnav teaching where the student follows the procedure of the task, arrives at the desired upon destination however, they have not thought about any of the processes and therefore are unlikely to understand the work they have been doing.

Too often teachers see a supported student and think they have support, I don't need to worry about them now. This then means the teacher is relying on the education support staff member being able to follow their instruction, while managing and supporting this student with additional needs.
The support which exists to close the achievement gap has effectively widened it by caring too much.

Trained and supported TAs, either working on a one to one basis or in a small group, helped primary-aged children with literacy and language problems to make statistically significant gains in learning when compared to similar children who did not receive TA support. (Farrell et al., 2010)
Unless the teacher guides the support that is occurring in the classroom, that support has the risk of actually having a negative impact on the students learning progress.
Our staff were too helpful. They wanted so much for the students to succeed that they would do things like tell the student exactly what to write or prompt them too quickly after starting work.

Education support staff see everything! Having them as the eyes and ears to inform about what is actually happening in classrooms rather than just relying on what is documented is an incredibly underrated resource for schools.
